### Inference for Categorical Variables

Earlier this week we considered comparisons of multiple group means, where groups are determined by some categorical variable

::: fragment

Now, consider the situation where:

:::

-   **Response variable**: categorical

-   **Explanatory variable**: categorical

-   **Parameter of interest**: $p_1 - p_2$?

    -   This parameter of interest only makes sense if **both** variables only have two categories.

::: fragment
We'll learn how to study the relationship between two categorical variables when **at least one has more than two categories.**
:::

<br>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Hypotheses

::: nonincremental

Consider the situation where:

-   **Response variable**: categorical
-   **Explanatory variable**: categorical
-   At least one of these has more than 2 categories

:::

::: fragment

$H_0$: The two variables are independent.

$H_a$: The two variables are dependent.

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Eyesight Example {.smaller}

Near-sightedness typically develops during the childhood years. [Quinn, Shin, Maguire, and Stone (1999)](https://www.nature.com/articles/20094) explored whether there is a relationship between the type of light children were exposed to at night and their eye health. Data was collected via questionnaires filled out by the children's parents at a university pediatric ophthalmology clinic.

::: fragment

::: columns

::: {.column width=35%}

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(infer)

# Import data
eye_data <- read_csv("data/eye_lighting.csv")

# Contingency table
eye_data %>%
  count(Lighting, Eye)
```

:::

::: {.column width=65%}

```{r fig.height=4}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(data = eye_data, 
       mapping = aes(x = Lighting,
                     fill = Eye)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.title = element_text(size=15))
```

:::

:::

:::

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

- **Discuss with Neighbors**: 
    - Does there appear to be a relationship/dependence?
    - What would we expect to see if there were no relationship/dependence? Would each block in the barchart be the same size?
    - Informally, how could we quantify how "typical" our sample is compared to what we'd see if there were no relationship/dependence?
    
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(3)
```


------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Test Statistic

To formally test whether there is a dependency, we need a test statistic!

-   Won't be a single sample statistic.

-   Needs to measure the **discrepancy between the observed sample and the sample we'd expect to see if $H_0$ (no relationship) were true**.

-   Would be nice if its null distribution could be approximated by a known probability model.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sample Result Tables

::: columns
::: column
#### Observed Sample Table

<br><br>

```{r}
table(eye_data$Eye, eye_data$Lighting) %>%
  addmargins() %>%
  kable(format = "html")
```
:::

::: column
#### Expected Sample Table

**Question**: If $H_0$ were correct, is this the table that we'd expect to see?

```{r, echo=FALSE}
Ho_dat <- data.frame(Eye = rep(c("Far", "Near", "Normal"), times = 53*3),
                     Lighting = rep(c("dark", "night", "room"), each = 53*3))
table(Ho_dat$Eye, Ho_dat$Lighting) %>%
  addmargins() %>%
  kable(format = "html")
```
:::
:::

## Sample Result Tables

::: columns
::: column
#### Observed Sample Table

<br><br>

```{r}
table(eye_data$Eye, eye_data$Lighting) %>%
  addmargins() %>%
  kable(format = "html")
```
:::

::: column
#### Expected Sample Table

Want a $H_0$ table that respects the overall eye condition proportions:

$$\hat{p}_{far} = 91/479$$

$$\hat{p}_{nor} = 251/479$$

$$\hat{p}_{nea} = 137/479$$
:::
:::

<br><br>

::: fragment

But we would expect that those with each eye condition are equally distributed across treatment conditions (`Lighting`)

:::

::: columns

#### Observed Sample Table

table(eye_data$Eye, eye_data$Lighting) %>%
  addmargins() %>%

```

**Question**: If $H_0$ were correct, what table would we expect to see?

  addmargins() %>%
  kable(format = "html")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Expected Table

::: columns
::: column

**Our observed sample**

```{r, fig.height = 8, echo = FALSE}
ggplot(data = eye_data, 
       mapping = aes(x = Lighting,
                     fill = Eye)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.title = element_text(size=15),
        legend.text = element_text(size=12))
```
:::

::: column

**Sample we'd expect under $H_0$**

```{r, fig.height = 8, echo = FALSE}
chisq.test(table(eye_data$Eye, eye_data$Lighting))$exp %>%
  as_tibble(rownames = "Eye") %>%
  pivot_longer(2:4, names_to = "Lighting") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = Lighting, fill = Eye, y = value)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.title = element_text(size=15),
        legend.text = element_text(size=12))
```
:::
:::

- **Q**: If the null is true, should we expect our sample to look *exactly* like the right graph? 


------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Test Statistic

Want the test statistic to quantify the difference between the observed table and the expected table.

::: columns
::: column
|        | dark | night | room | Sum |
|:-------|-----:|------:|-----:|----:|
| Far    |   40 |    39 |   12 |  91 |
| Near   |   18 |    78 |   41 | 137 |
| Normal |  114 |   115 |   22 | 251 |
| Sum    |  172 |   232 |   75 | 479 |
:::

::: column
|        |   dark |  night |  room | Sum |
|:-------|-------:|-------:|------:|----:|
| Far    |  32.68 |  44.08 | 14.25 |  91 |
| Near   |  49.19 |  66.35 | 21.45 | 137 |
| Normal |  90.13 | 121.57 | 39.30 | 251 |
| Sum    | 172.00 | 232.00 | 75.00 | 479 |
:::
:::

<br>

::: fragment
For each cell, compute how far our observation is from the expected value, relative to the expected value:

```{=tex}
\begin{align*}
\mbox{Cell Difference} &= \frac{\mbox{observed - expected}}{\sqrt{\mbox{expected}}}
\end{align*}
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Test Statistic

Want the test statistic to quantify the difference between the observed table and the expected table.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
round(chisq.test(table(eye_data$Eye, eye_data$Lighting))$residuals, 2) %>%
  kable(format = "html")
```

<br>

This is the cell-by-cell difference between our distributions, but our test statistic should be a single number. **How should we summarize these?**

```{=tex}
\begin{align*}
\mbox{Cell Difference} &= \frac{\mbox{observed - expected}}{\sqrt{\mbox{expected}}}
\end{align*}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Test Statistic

**Test Statistic Formula:** We can sum the squares of the cell-wise differences (this results in nice theoretical properties)

```{=tex}
\begin{align*}
\chi^2 = \sum \left(\frac{\mbox{observed - expected}}{\sqrt{\mbox{expected}}} \right)^2
\end{align*}
```
```{r}
#| output-location: column

library(infer)
#Compute Chi-square test stat
test_stat <- eye_data %>%
  specify(Eye ~ Lighting) %>%
  calculate(stat = "Chisq") 
test_stat
```

<br>

**Questions:**

1.  Is a test statistic **unusual** if it is a large number or a small number?
2.  What do we require to be able to assess if 56.5 **unusual** under $H_0$?


```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(2)
```

### The Null Distribution: Simulation-based

1. Copy our original data set, but randomly shuffle (aka "permute") the treatment condition (`Lighting`)
2. Calculate our chi-squared statistic on the shuffled data set
3. Repeat 1-2 many times! 

::: fragment

```{r}
# Construct null distribution
null_dist <- eye_data %>%
  specify(Eye ~ Lighting) %>%
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>%
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") %>%
  calculate(stat = "Chisq")


visualize(null_dist)
```

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The Null Distribution: Simulation-based

**Make key observations about the distribution with your neighbor(s)**:

- What's the smallest possible value? Does this make sense?

- How would you describe the shape? What does this imply for inference? 

- Is our observed test statistic of 56.5 unusual?

- Guess the p-value given our test statistic.

::: columns

::: {.column width=65%}

```{r, fig.height = 4, echo = FALSE}
visualize(null_dist)
```

:::

::: {.column width=35%}

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

- **Our p-value**:

```{r echo = TRUE}
mean(null_dist$stat >= 56.5)
```


:::

:::

:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(3)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Approximating the Null Distribution

If there are at least 5 observations in each cell, then our test statistic approximately follows a particular distribution:

$$
\mbox{test statistic} \sim \chi^2(df = (k - 1)(j - 1))
$$ where $k$ is the number of categories in the response variable and $j$ is the number of categories in the explanatory variable.

<br>

The $df$ controls the center and spread of the distribution.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The Chi-Squared Test

Under these conditions, we can use R to quickly run a theory-based Chi-squared test:

```{r echo = TRUE}
chisq.test(eye_data$Eye, eye_data$Lighting)
```

<br><br>

::: {.columns .fragment .nonincremental}

::: {.column  .nonincremental}

-   **Q**: Conclusions from our hypothesis test?

-   **Q**: Causal link between room lighting at bedtime and eye conditions?

:::

::: column

```{r fig.height=5}
ggplot(data = eye_data, 
       mapping = aes(x = Lighting,
                     fill = Eye)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.title = element_text(size=15),
        legend.text = element_text(size=16))
```


:::

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The Chi-Squared Test - Related Applications

- We can apply a similar idea to check "goodness-of-fit" for counts of one categorical variable
    - Ex. Does the distribution of first digits in some financial data follow Benford's Law? (fraud detection)
    - Are traffic accidents uniformally distributed across days of the week?
